stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Masala Dosa in Karnataka & the South
stages.narrative: The dosa has ancient beginnings in South India and Karnataka. A preparation named 'dosaka' is first documented in the 12th-century Sanskrit work Manasollasa, compiled by King Someshvara III of the Western Chalukya dynasty ruling northern Karnataka. In early times, dosas were thick, soft griddle-cakes cooked on clay plates using fermented black gram and rice batter. The dish evolved deeply within the temple kitchens of Udupi and Old Mysore, where natural overnight fermentation was perfected into an art.

Ancient culinary form: Originally thick, spongy, and unfermented or purely pulse-based griddle-cakes baked on earthen plates.
Temple heritage: Perfected in Udupi Madhwa temple kitchens through stone-ground wild fermentation of rice and black gram.
Cooking method: Naturally aerated batter swirled on griddles over wood hearths into soft, wholesome breakfast cakes.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Masala Dosa Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: Sona Masuri rice, urad dal, fenugreek seeds, poha, potatoes, onions, green chillies, mustard seeds, curry leaves, pure desi ghee or butter.

1. Soak Sona Masuri rice, urad dal, fenugreek seeds, and poha in water for 5 hours, then grind in a wet grinder to a silky, aerated batter.
2. Add salt, mix thoroughly with hands to introduce natural microflora, and ferment overnight in a warm spot for 8 to 12 hours.

stages.headline: Birth of Bisi Bele Bath in Karnataka & the Mysore Palace
stages.narrative: Bisi Bele Bath originates from the royal kitchens of the Mysore Palace under the Wodeyar dynasty in southern Karnataka. The name translates in Kannada to 'hot lentil rice' (bisi = hot, bele = lentil, bath = rice preparation). Palace cooks formulated it as an elaborate, wholesome royal offering to the palace deities, combining short-grain rice with toor dal, wild forest spices, aged tamarind, and desi ghee. From the Mysore court, the dish was embraced by Karnataka's temple traditions and Madhwa community kitchens, establishing its iconic status across the state.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Bisi Bele Bath Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: Sona Masuri rice, toor dal, mixed vegetables (carrots, beans, peas), tamarind extract, jaggery, Byadagi dry red chillies, kapok buds (marathi moggu), dry coconut (copra), cashew nuts, pure desi ghee.

1. Rinse Sona Masuri rice and toor dal together, then pressure-cook with water and a pinch of turmeric for 4 to 5 whistles until soft and easily mashable.
2. Dry-roast Byadagi chillies, chana dal, urad dal, coriander seeds, cumin, fenugreek, marathi moggu, and cinnamon until aromatic; add grated copra and hing, cool, and grind into a fine bisi bele bath spice powder.
3. Boil chopped carrots, French beans, potatoes, peas, and shallots in water with salt until tender.
4. Add thick tamarind extract, grated jaggery, and 3 tablespoons of the prepared spice powder to the cooked vegetables and simmer for 5 minutes.
5. Lightly mash the cooked rice and dal, then combine them into the bubbling spiced vegetable broth.
6. Adjust consistency with warm water to a smooth, pourable porridge and simmer on low heat for 7 minutes, stirring gently to prevent sticking.
7. Heat pure desi ghee in a pan, crackle mustard seeds and curry leaves, and fry cashew nuts and broken dried chillies until golden.
8. Pour the sizzling ghee tempering over the bisi bele bath, mix well, rest for 2 minutes, and serve piping hot topped with crisp kara boondi.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Indori Poha: Origin & Street Food Heritage
stages.narrative:
Indori poha is a famous breakfast and street food of Indore, in Madhya Pradesh. Poha is the Hindi name for flattened rice. "Indori" means "of Indore". Poha is a widely eaten Indian food. What makes this version Indori is how it is cooked and topped. Unlike many other poha styles, it is steamed instead of being cooked directly with other ingredients, and the onions are not sauteed. Chopped raw onions go on top. It is finished with toppings such as sev, masala boondi (nukti), pomegranate and jeeravan masala, and is often served with hot jalebi. No reliable historical record gives the exact year, place or creator of Indori poha. One popular account says rulers from Maharashtra brought poha to this region, but this is not documented.

Why it is famous:
- Its own cooking style: the poha is steamed, which gives it a distinct soft texture and taste.
- Balanced flavour: sweet, tangy and spicy together, with fennel seeds adding a light sweetness.
- Many textures in one plate: soft poha, crunchy sev and boondi, fresh onion and juicy pomegranate.
- Jeeravan masala: a spice blend from Madhya Pradesh whose taste is different from chaat masala or garam masala.
- Poha-jalebi: hot, sweet jalebi with savoury poha is the classic Indore pairing.
- Morning street food: vendors across Indore sell it in the morning, often next to kachori and samosa.
- Wide reach: it is also sold in nearby cities such as Ujjain, Dewas, Ratlam and Bhopal, and is becoming popular in other states.

stages.headline: Indori Poha Recipe: 12 Key Ingredients, 10 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: Thick or medium-thick poha (flattened rice), Turmeric, sugar and salt, Oil, Mustard seeds and fennel seeds, Green chilli, Onion (raw, chopped), Fresh coriander leaves, Jeeravan masala, Ratlami or Indori sev, and masala boondi (nukti), Lemon, Pomegranate (optional), Hot jalebi (for serving, optional).

1. Rinse the poha. - Rinse thick poha in a strainer under clean running water. Do not over-rinse, or it turns mushy.
2. Drain and rest. - Drain well. The flakes should be soft but whole. If still firm, sprinkle a little water and wait a few minutes.
3. Add the dry seasoning. - Add turmeric, sugar and salt to the poha and mix lightly.
4. Make the tempering. - Heat oil on low to medium-low heat. Add mustard seeds, then fennel seeds, then green chilli.
5. Add the poha. - Keep the heat low and mix gently until the colour turns light yellow.
6. Steam the poha. - Cover with a lid and steam on low heat for about 1 to 2 minutes. Stir and switch off the heat.
7. Plate it hot. - Take the hot poha on a plate.
8. Add the fresh toppings. - Top with chopped raw onion and coriander, sprinkle jeeravan masala, and add pomegranate.
9. Add the crunch. - Top with masala boondi (nukti) and Ratlami or Indori sev.
10. Finish and serve. - Squeeze lemon juice on top. Serve straight away, with hot jalebi.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Bhutte Ka Kees: Origin & Malwa Heritage
stages.narrative:
Bhutte Ka Kees is a famous street food and traditional delicacy of Madhya Pradesh, especially celebrated across the Malwa region including Indore (famous in Sarafa Bazaar night market and Chappan Dukan). "Bhutta" means corn on the cob, and "Kees" comes from "keesna" (to grate in Hindi). Fresh tender corn kernels are grated fresh, releasing sweet corn pulp and juice, then slow-braised in full-cream milk, tempered with mustard seeds, cumin, hing (asafoetida), and green chillies, and finished with freshly grated coconut, coriander, and lemon juice. No reliable historical record gives the exact year, place or creator of Bhutte Ka Kees, though local tradition associates it with Holkar-era royal banquets and Malwa monsoon harvest feasts.

Why it is famous:
- Its own cooking style: fresh corn is grated to extract juices and slow-braised in milk, yielding a luscious creamy and grainy texture.
- Balanced flavour: natural corn sweetness harmonized with spicy green chillies, aromatic hing, and tangy fresh lemon.
- Night street food royalty: an iconic attraction at Indore's legendary Sarafa Bazaar and Chappan Dukan.
- Seasonal harvest celebration: traditionally crafted during monsoons when tender desi bhutta is harvested in Malwa.
- Rich garnishes: served steaming hot topped with freshly grated coconut, coriander, crunchy sev, and a dash of jeeravan masala.
- Wide reach: popular across Indore, Ujjain, Ratlam, Bhopal, and now featured on menus nationwide.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Recipe: 12 Key Ingredients & 10 Preparation Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: Fresh tender sweet corn (bhutta, grated), Full cream milk, Desi ghee or oil, Mustard seeds and cumin seeds (jeera), Asafoetida (hing), Green chillies (finely chopped), Fresh ginger (grated), Turmeric powder, Sugar and salt, Fresh coconut (scraped/grated), Fresh coriander leaves, Lemon (for tang) and jeeravan masala / sev (optional).

1. Grate the corn. - Husk fresh tender corn cobs and grate using a medium grater to collect pulp and juices.
2. Heat the fat. - Heat ghee or oil in a heavy kadhai over medium-low heat.
3. Splutter the spices. - Add mustard seeds and cumin seeds; once they crackle, add asafoetida (hing).
4. Sauté the aromatics. - Add finely chopped green chillies and grated ginger; sauté for 30 seconds until aromatic.
5. Cook the corn pulp. - Add grated corn, turmeric powder, salt, and a pinch of sugar; sauté on low heat for 3-4 minutes.
6. Pour the milk. - Slowly pour in full cream milk while stirring continuously to blend evenly.
7. Simmer and thicken. - Cover with a lid and cook on low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until milk is absorbed and corn is tender.
8. Stir in fresh garnish. - Turn off the heat and stir in half of the freshly grated coconut and chopped coriander leaves.
9. Season to taste. - Squeeze fresh lemon juice and dust with jeeravan masala for signature Indori tang.
10. Finish and serve. - Spoon hot into bowls, garnish with remaining grated coconut, coriander, and crispy sev.

Use fresh tender corn. Grating rather than blending retains the quintessential texture. Add milk gradually on low heat to achieve creamy consistency.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Dal Bafla: Origin & Festive Malwa Heritage
stages.narrative:
Dal Bafla is the signature celebratory feast of Madhya Pradesh, celebrated throughout the Malwa and Bundelkhand regions (notably in Ujjain, Indore, Ratlam, and Maheshwar). It is related to Rajasthani baati but distinguished by its unique two-stage cooking: dough balls of coarse whole-wheat flour, semolina, and ghee are boiled in spiced water first, then roasted over cow-dung embers or baked in an oven until blistered and golden. The boiling gelatinizes the starch, ensuring the inside remains incredibly tender and fluffy, while the baking creates a crisp outer crust. Hot baflas are cracked open, drenched completely in melted desi ghee, and paired with spicy five-lentil Panchmel Dal, fiery garlic chutney, and sweet churma.

Why it is famous:
- Unique boil-then-bake method: boiling before baking ensures a soft, tender crumb unlike the firmer, dry Rajasthani baati.
- Desi ghee immersion: hot baflas are cracked open and fully bathed in warm desi ghee, soaking up rich aroma.
- Panchmel Dal accompaniment: served with a harmonious blend of five pulses (toor, moong, chana, urad, masoor) tempered with hing and cumin.
- Sacred banquet centerpiece: standard community meal at weddings, festivals, and pilgrimage feasts across Malwa and the Narmada valley.
- Complex accompaniments: traditionally paired with fiery raw garlic chutney, sweet churma or laddu, and tangy kadhi.
- Wide cultural reverence: celebrated in thali restaurants and royal heritage banquets across Central India.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Recipe: 12 Key Ingredients & 10 Preparation Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: Coarse whole-wheat flour (atta), Semolina (sooji / rava), Pure desi ghee, Ajwain (carom seeds), Turmeric powder and pinch of baking soda, Panchmel dal (toor, chana, moong, urad, masoor), Tomatoes and green chillies, Fresh ginger (grated), Cumin seeds and mustard seeds, Asafoetida (hing), Fresh coriander leaves, Spicy red garlic chutney & lemon wedges.

1. Make the dough. - Mix coarse wheat flour, sooji, ajwain, turmeric, salt, and melted ghee (moyen). Rub until crumbly, then knead into a stiff dough with warm water.
2. Shape the baflas. - Divide dough into smooth, medium round balls and make a slight dimple in the center with your thumb.
3. Boil water. - In a large pot, bring water to a rolling boil with 1/2 tsp turmeric and salt.
4. Boil the baflas. - Gently lower the dough balls into boiling water and cook for 12-15 minutes until they float to the surface.
5. Drain and dry. - Lift baflas out with a slotted spoon and dry on a clean towel for 5-10 minutes.
6. Bake until crisp. - Bake in a preheated baati oven or conventional oven at 200°C (390°F) for 20-25 minutes, turning until golden and blistered.
7. Cook the dal. - Pressure cook mixed five lentils with turmeric and salt until soft and creamy.
8. Temper the dal. - Heat ghee in a pan, crackle cumin and mustard seeds, add hing, green chillies, ginger, tomatoes, and spices; pour into dal.
9. Crush and ghee-soak. - Gently crush the hot baked baflas in a napkin and immerse them completely in a bowl of warm desi ghee.
10. Assemble and serve. - Serve piping hot ghee-drenched baflas with Panchmel dal, fiery garlic chutney, sliced onions, and lemon.

Boiling before baking is mandatory for authentic bafla texture. Submerge baflas in ghee while piping hot for complete absorption.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Makki di Roti & Sarson da Saag: Agrarian Winter Heritage
stages.narrative:
Makki di roti and sarson da saag is a famous winter staple and comfort food of Punjab. "Makki" means maize or corn, "roti" means flatbread, and "sarson" is the Hindi and Punjabi name for mustard greens. "Saag" refers to cooked leafy greens. It is an agricultural hearth food traditionally cooked during the cold harvest months when fresh mustard leaves are abundant in the fields. The greens are slow-cooked and churned into a thick, coarse mash, while the flatbread is hand-patted from coarse maize flour and griddled on a tawa. It is finished with a generous dollop of freshly churned white butter (makhan) and served with jaggery (gur). No reliable historical record gives the exact year, place or creator of this combination; it has been a rural staple across Punjabi farming households for generations.

Why it is famous:
- Seasonal harmony: fresh winter mustard greens paired with hearty yellow corn flatbread.
- Earthy, robust flavour: mild natural bitterness of mustard greens balanced by sweet jaggery and rich churned butter.
- Traditional churning: slow-cooked greens mashed with a wooden churner (ghotna) produce a distinct rustic texture.
- Gluten-free flatbread technique: hand-patted cornmeal dough griddled until golden and crisp on the edges.
- Classic accompaniment: served with white butter and jaggery, creating a comforting sweet-savoury balance.
- Hearty farm nutrition: traditionally eaten by farmers for energy and warmth through long winter days.
- Wide popularity: a signature emblem of Punjabi hospitality enjoyed across roadside dhabas and homes throughout northern India.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Makki di Roti & Sarson da Saag Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 10 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: Fresh mustard greens (sarson), Spinach (palak) and bathua leaves, Maize flour (makki ka atta), Fresh ginger, garlic and green chillies, Onions, Mustard oil or ghee, Salt, Warm water, Fresh white butter (makhan), Jaggery (gur, for serving).

1. Clean and chop the greens. - Wash mustard, spinach and bathua leaves thoroughly in running water to remove grit, then chop them finely.
2. Simmer the greens. - Place the chopped greens in a heavy pot with salt, green chillies, ginger and garlic, and simmer on low heat until tender.
3. Churn the saag. - Mash the softened greens using a traditional wooden churner (ghotna) or hand masher until coarse and thick.
4. Add the maize flour thickener. - Sprinkle a little maize flour into the simmering greens and churn continuously to prevent lumps from forming.
5. Cook the tempering. - Heat ghee or mustard oil in a separate pan. Sauté chopped onions, garlic and ginger until golden brown.
6. Combine and simmer. - Pour the hot tempering into the mashed greens. Stir well and simmer on low heat for a few minutes.
7. Prepare the makki dough. - Mix maize flour with a pinch of salt and gradually add warm water. Knead into a soft, pliable dough.
8. Pat the flatbread. - Divide the dough into balls and pat gently between wet palms or on parchment paper into a round flatbread.
9. Griddle on the tawa. - Transfer carefully to a hot tawa. Cook on medium heat with a little ghee until both sides have golden spots and turn crisp.
10. Finish and serve hot. - Plate the hot makki di roti next to a steaming bowl of sarson da saag. Top with a generous dollop of white butter and serve with jaggery.

Traditional saag combines mustard greens with spinach or bathua to balance bitterness. Always knead maize flour with warm water for easier shaping.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Butter Chicken: Origin & Tandoori Heritage
stages.narrative:
Butter chicken, traditionally known as murgh makhani, is one of the most celebrated dishes of Punjabi and northern Indian cuisine. "Murgh" means chicken, and "makhani" refers to butter, describing a preparation enriched with churned butter and cream. The dish originated from post-partition refugee kitchens where cooks sought a way to revive tandoor-roasted chicken pieces that became dry. Leftover tandoor-charred chicken was gently simmered in a velvety, rich sauce made from ripe tomatoes, butter, cream and gentle spices. The combination of smoky, charred tandoori chicken pieces with a silky, mildly sweet and tangy tomato-butter gravy became an immediate sensation. While popular tradition connects its creation to restaurant kitchens in northern India, exact personal origins remain contested and unverified in official culinary records.

Why it is famous:
- Silky texture: a smooth, strained tomato gravy enriched with fresh butter and dairy cream.
- Smoky char balance: the smokiness of tandoor-roasted chicken cuts cleanly through the creamy gravy.
- Balanced mild spices: aromatic rather than searingly spicy, with green cardamom, Kashmiri chilli and dried fenugreek.
- Kasuri methi finish: crushed dried fenugreek leaves impart a distinct earthy fragrance essential to the dish.
- Global popularity: widely recognized and served in Indian restaurants worldwide as a quintessential comfort dish.
- Tandoor heritage: celebrates the Punjabi tandoor technique of high-heat clay oven roasting.
- Classic pairings: traditionally enjoyed with hot garlic naan, tandoori roti, or fragrant basmati rice.

The combination of smoky, charred tandoori chicken pieces with a silky, mildly sweet and tangy tomato-butter gravy became an immediate sensation.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Butter Chicken Recipe: 11 Key Ingredients, 10 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: Chicken (boneless pieces or bone-in cuts), Hung curd (thick yogurt), Ginger-garlic paste, Kashmiri red chilli powder and turmeric, Ripe tomatoes, Butter and ghee, Fresh dairy cream, Kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves), Whole spices (green cardamom, cinnamon, cloves), Salt and a pinch of sugar, Lemon juice.

1. Marinate the chicken. - Coat chicken pieces with curd, ginger-garlic paste, Kashmiri red chilli, lemon juice and salt. Rest for at least 30 minutes.
2. Roast the chicken. - Cook the marinated chicken in a hot tandoor, oven or heavy pan until lightly charred and cooked through. Set aside.
3. Simmer the tomato base. - In a pot, cook chopped ripe tomatoes with whole spices, ginger, garlic and a little water until soft and pulpy.
4. Blend and strain. - Cool the tomato mixture, blend until smooth, and pass through a sieve to achieve a velvety texture.
5. Heat the butter. - Melt butter and a little ghee in a pan on low to medium-low heat. Add a pinch of Kashmiri chilli for colour.
6. Add the strained sauce. - Pour the smooth tomato purée into the butter. Simmer gently until the gravy thickens and oil begins to separate.
7. Add the roasted chicken. - Add the charred chicken pieces to the simmering sauce and mix gently so the meat absorbs the flavours.
8. Season and balance. - Add salt, a pinch of sugar to balance acidity, and gentle garam masala. Simmer on low heat for 5 minutes.
9. Finish with cream and fenugreek. - Stir in fresh dairy cream and crushed kasuri methi between your palms. Switch off the heat.
10. Serve hot. - Garnish with a swirl of fresh cream and a pat of melting butter. Serve with hot tandoori roti or naan.

Straining the tomato puree is key to achieving the signature velvety texture. Kasuri methi should always be crushed lightly before adding.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Amritsari Kulcha: Tandoor Stuffed Bread Heritage
stages.narrative:
Amritsari kulcha is a famous tandoor-baked stuffed flatbread originating from the city of Amritsar, in Punjab. "Kulcha" is a traditional northern Indian leavened or layered flatbread made from refined wheat flour. It is particularly famous around the bustling food lanes and street eateries surrounding the historic center of Amritsar. The dough is laminated with ghee or fat, stuffed with a spicy mixture of mashed potatoes, onions and pomegranate seeds, and baked inside a searing clay tandoor. When pulled crisp and blistering from the tandoor wall, the bread is crushed by hand so the flaky layers shatter, then crowned with fresh white butter. It is traditionally paired with spicy chickpea curry (chole), tangy tamarind-onion chutney (pyaz ki chutney), and pickles. No reliable historical record documents the exact year or creator of the stuffed Amritsari kulcha; it evolved through Punjab's urban tandoor-baking tradition.

Why it is famous:
- Shattering flaky texture: multiple rolled and laminated layers create an irresistible crisp and flaky crust.
- Tandoor char: slapped directly onto the inner clay walls of a high-heat tandoor, giving it blistered spots and a smoky flavour.
- Spicy potato filling: spiced with crushed coriander seeds, anardana (dried pomegranate), carom seeds (ajwain), and green chillies.
- Hand-crushed service: bakers crush the hot bread between their palms before serving to reveal the flaky interior.
- Melting butter crown: generously topped with fresh homemade white butter that melts through the hot shattered layers.
- Iconic breakfast pairing: eaten with spicy Punjabi chole and tangy sliced onion chutney for a filling morning meal.
- Street food pilgrimage: a beloved culinary hallmark that visitors from all over the world seek in Amritsar.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Amritsari Kulcha Recipe: 11 Key Ingredients, 10 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: Refined wheat flour (maida), Boiled and mashed potatoes, Ghee or butter (for lamination and topping), Carom seeds (ajwain) and cumin, Crushed coriander seeds, Dried pomegranate seeds (anardana powder), Green chilli and fresh coriander, Chopped onion, Salt, Water (for kneading), Fresh white butter (for serving).

1. Knead the dough. - Mix refined flour, a pinch of salt and water. Knead into a soft, smooth dough, cover with a damp cloth, and rest for 30 minutes.
2. Laminate the layers. - Roll the dough flat, smear generously with ghee, fold in thirds like an envelope, and repeat to build flaky layers.
3. Prepare the filling. - Mash boiled potatoes with chopped onion, green chilli, fresh coriander, crushed coriander seeds, anardana, ajwain and salt.
4. Portion and stuff. - Divide the layered dough into balls. Flatten each ball slightly, place a generous portion of stuffing in the centre, and seal tightly.
5. Roll and flatten. - Gently pat or roll the stuffed dough with your fingers into a thick round disc, taking care not to tear the edges.
6. Apply moisture and herbs. - Wet the top with a splash of water and press fresh coriander and crushed coriander seeds onto the surface.
7. Bake in tandoor or tawa. - Press the wet side onto the hot inner tandoor wall or an inverted hot iron tawa so it sticks firmly.
8. Crisp both sides. - Cook until the base is firmly set, then invert the tawa directly over the open flame until blisters turn golden brown and crisp.
9. Hand-crush for layers. - Carefully remove the blistering kulcha and crush it gently between your palms to crack the flaky layers open.
10. Butter and serve. - Top immediately with a melting dollop of fresh white butter. Serve piping hot with spicy chole and tamarind onion chutney.

Coarsely crushed coriander seeds and anardana in the stuffing provide the signature Amritsari crunch and tang. Do not use non-stick pans if baking on a tawa.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Hyderabadi Dum Biryani Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: basmati rice, mutton or chicken, curd, fried onions, ginger-garlic paste, green chillies, whole spices and garam masala, mint and coriander, saffron milk, ghee.

1. Marinate the meat with curd, spices, ginger-garlic paste, herbs and fried onions. Mix well and rest it (overnight for best flavour, or a few hours).
2. Fry the onions until golden brown and crisp. Keep some aside for layering.
3. Parboil the rice with whole spices and salt until about 70% cooked (the grain should break easily but still feel firm inside). Drain it.
4. Layer the marinated meat at the bottom of a heavy pot, then spread the rice evenly on top.
5. Top with fried onions, mint, coriander, saffron milk and ghee.
6. Seal the lid tightly with dough or foil so no steam escapes.
7. Cook on high heat for a few minutes until steam builds, then on low heat for about 40 minutes (dum).
8. Rest for 10 minutes without opening, then mix gently from the sides and serve with raita.

stages.title: Origin
stages.headline: Birth of Hyderabadi Haleem in Telangana & the Deccan
stages.narrative: Haleem traces its ancestry to the medieval Arab dish harees, a slow-cooked porridge of pounded meat and wheat. It was introduced to Hyderabad by the Arab diaspora (Chaush soldiers from Yemen) serving in the irregular army of the Asaf Jahi Nizams. In the royal kitchens of the Nizams and Paigah nobles, the rustic harees was refined and Indianized by introducing aromatic Deccan spices, mixed lentils, ghee, dry fruits, and rose petals. It became the signature delicacy of Hyderabad, especially cherished during Ramzan for breaking the fast.

Royal court refinement: In the royal kitchens of the Nizams and Paigah nobles, the rustic harees was refined with local Deccan spices, mixed lentils, pure ghee, dry fruits, and rose petals.
Cultural tradition: Cooked overnight in large wood-fired copper degs and served as the preeminent energy-replenishing dish to break the fast during Ramzan.
Cooking method: Slow-simmered for 8 to 12 hours and vigorously pounded with heavy wooden pestles (ghotni) until meat and wheat merge into a smooth, cohesive porridge.

stages.title: Recipe
stages.headline: Hyderabadi Haleem Recipe: 10 Key Ingredients, 8 Steps
stages.narrative:
Key ingredients: broken wheat (dalia), boneless mutton, chana and moong lentils, curd, pure desi ghee, fried onions (birista), ginger-garlic paste, whole spices and garam masala, mint and coriander, almonds and cashew nuts.

1. Soak broken wheat and lentils (chana and moong) in water for 1 to 2 hours, then drain.
2. Marinate the mutton with curd, ginger-garlic paste, turmeric, chilli powder, salt, and half of the garam masala for at least 1 hour.
3. In a heavy pot or pressure cooker, heat ghee and saute whole spices (shahi jeera, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon) and a portion of fried onions until fragrant.
4. Add the marinated meat and sear on medium-high heat, then add water and pressure-cook or slow-simmer until the meat is thoroughly tender and falling apart.
5. Separately boil the soaked broken wheat and lentils with a pinch of turmeric and water until completely soft and mushy.
6. Shred the cooked meat off any bones and combine the shredded meat and its rich broth into the pot of cooked wheat and lentils.
7. Slow-simmer over low heat while vigorously mashing and pounding with a wooden masher (ghotni) for 30–40 minutes, gradually incorporating hot ghee until the mixture turns silky, elastic, and pasty.
8. Season with remaining garam masala, mint, and coriander; ladle into warm bowls and top with hot ghee, golden fried onions, toasted cashews, and fresh lemon wedges.
